clue.text: Fighting man with reserve, presumably?

parts.note: surface reading: a soldier held back in the reserve forces
setter's reading: a rank-and-file soldier who is reserved, keeping himself to himself

explanation.surface: A soldier kept back in reserve, ready to be called up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' suggests the reserve army, but the joke is reticence: someone private keeps their own counsel.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest army rank is private, and a private person is reserved, so the phrase covers both senses.

clue.text: Fast food processor

parts.note: surface reading: a kitchen gadget for chopping, or a burger chain
setter's reading: an appliance that cooks food quickly under steam pressure

explanation.surface: A kitchen machine, or a factory turning out burgers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast food' reads as junk food, and 'food processor' as a blender; split differently it is a pan that cooks food fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealed pan that uses steam pressure cooks meals quickly, processing food at speed.

clue.text: Means whereby, perhaps, new dentist extracts tooth initially

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters are one possible arrangement, so they may be reordered
a dentist who extracts pulls something out, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
taken as written

indicators.note: 'initially' points to the very start of the word beside it

parts.note: the first letter of tooth

explanation.surface: A dentist pulls out a tooth, describing the method used.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one T out of DENTIST, add N, and rearrange the seven letters to INTENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean something is to have it as your purpose, so 'means' and 'intends' are verb synonyms.

clue.text: Sat out with Israeli acrobats

indicators.note: 'out' suggests things turned out of their places, so the letters are scattered and reset

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sat out of a performance alongside some Israeli acrobats.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerialists perform high in the air on trapezes and wires, a kind of circus acrobat.

clue.text: Charm shown by object attracting attention

parts.note: an end is an aim or purpose, as in 'to that end'
to have someone's ear, or lend an ear, is to have their attention

explanation.surface: A charm or trinket that draws people's notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attracting' is only a joining word: the purpose sits in front of the attention.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm someone is to win their affection, which is exactly what endearing yourself does; both are verbs.

clue.text: Set one trap in exam first of all

indicators.note: to set something in a place is to put it there, so these go inside the exam

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination
the Roman numeral for one
a gin is a snare for catching game

explanation.surface: An examiner sets a trick question in a test paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of all' looks like an instruction to take initial letters, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something original is the earliest version, the one that came before every other.

clue.text: Idiot takes part in grand opera

indicators.note: taking part in something means being inside it, so the letters sit within the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A fool lands a role in a big operatic production.
explanation.definitionFit: A dope is informal for a stupid person, a fool or dimwit.

clue.text: Old country incredibly irate about XV-a-side game

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the jumbled letters surround the game
something done incredibly is beyond belief, so the letters end up in an unlikely order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
rugby union is played fifteen a side, abbreviated RU

explanation.surface: Someone becomes furious about a rugby match.
explanation.walkthrough: XV is the Roman numeral fifteen; rugby league has thirteen players, so the fifteen-a-side game is rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Etruria was the ancient land of the Etruscans in central Italy, before Rome absorbed it.

clue.text: One who operates on credit?

parts.note: surface reading: a trader or business that runs on borrowed money
setter's reading: credit cards are called plastic, and a surgeon operates

explanation.surface: A business that keeps going on borrowed money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' is slang for credit cards, and 'operates' turns the trader into a doctor in theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmetic or reconstructive doctor performs operations, and plastic is everyday slang for credit cards.

clue.text: Went in for contest and chopped tree, finally?

parts.note: finally means in the end

indicators.note: something chopped is cut into bits, so its letters are broken up and reset

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A lumberjack signs up for a competition and fells a tree at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled tree sits inside END; no word signals the insertion, which the question mark excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a race or competition is to put yourself forward as a competitor, so went in for matches entered.

clue.text: Jeopardise one fairy in 1050

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: 'in' places the fairy inside the number that follows it

parts.note: in Roman numerals M is 1000 and L is 50
a peri is a fairy of Persian legend, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale threat set in the year of the Norman era.
explanation.walkthrough: The fairy goes inside ML, and the one stands in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil something is to put it in danger, the same as jeopardising it; both are verbs.

clue.text: Christopher's vessel made by worker in old Biblical land?

indicators.note: 'in' puts the worker inside the land named after it

parts.note: Samaria was the region of ancient Israel in the Bible
the worker ant is a crossword staple

explanation.surface: A ship built by a labourer in the Holy Land.
explanation.definitionFit: The Santa Maria was the flagship of Christopher Columbus on his first voyage across the Atlantic in 1492.

clue.text: Crafts brought over from Australia

indicators.note: bringing something over flips it, so the letters run backwards
'from' says the letters are taken out of the word that follows

parts.note: four letters lie inside this word

explanation.surface: Handicrafts imported from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Read Australia backwards and ARTS appears in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Arts and crafts are skilled handiwork; arts here means creative skills, a plural noun like crafts.

clue.text: English region coming out against ale?

indicators.note: things coming out emerge in a new form, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A part of England protests against beer.
explanation.definitionFit: East Anglia is the bulge of eastern England covering Norfolk, Suffolk and parts of Cambridgeshire.

clue.text: Rock Curtis, countryman

indicators.note: to rock something is to shake it, so the letters are jolted out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rock musician called Curtis who grew up on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic is a person from the country, often simple or unsophisticated, so a noun for a rural dweller.

clue.text: Hair a man styled for Indian princess

indicators.note: hair that is styled is rearranged, so these letters are dressed in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A male hairdresser does an Indian royal's hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharani is the wife or widow of a maharaja, or a ruling queen in her own right in India.

clue.text: Get lower degree at Oxford? It's chilling!

parts.note: when it freezes the temperature drops to a low number of degrees
a student who is up is in residence at university

explanation.surface: A student settles for a poor class of degree at Oxford, which is horrifying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower degree' suggests a second-class university result; it is temperature. Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge means studying there.
explanation.definitionFit: A freeze-up is a spell of severe frost when water and ground ice over, so it is literally chilling.

clue.text: Remains in this place?

parts.note: surface reading: someone stays put, a verb
setter's reading: a noun for dead bodies, kept in a burial ground

explanation.surface: Someone stays where they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' reads as a verb; as a noun it means a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial ground is where the dead, called mortal remains, are laid to rest.

clue.text: Rifle aesthetic items in car

indicators.note: 'in' puts what comes before it inside the car

parts.note: the Mini is a classic small British car
works made to be beautiful are art

explanation.surface: A thief rifles through artworks stored in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rifle' looks like a verb for ransacking, but it is the gun. The Martini-Henry was a Victorian British army rifle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Martini was a single-shot breech-loading rifle used by the British army in the late nineteenth century.

clue.text: What may lead to unfortunate run-outs, nothing less?

definitions.text: What may lead to unfortunate run-outs, nothing less?

indicators.note: something unfortunate has gone wrong, so the letters come out in a mishap order
'less' means minus, so something is subtracted

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator on what causes batsmen to be run out.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the O from RUNOUTS and rearrange. In cricket a batsman turning back mid-run is easily run out, so the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman who turns round mid-run to scramble back can be stranded, so reversing direction often costs a wicket.

clue.text: Italian course which comes in parcels

definitions.text: Italian course which comes in parcels

parts.note: surface reading: a language class or a correspondence course posted in packages
setter's reading: a pasta dish of small stuffed squares, like tiny parcels

explanation.surface: A correspondence course in Italian arrives by post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests lessons and 'parcels' the post; both are about food.
explanation.definitionFit: This pasta dish consists of small square envelopes of dough filled with meat or cheese, served as a meal course.

clue.text: Change to tune musically sustained

indicators.note: to change something alters its form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician alters a melody so the notes are held longer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenuto is an Italian score marking telling the player to hold a note for its full value.

clue.text: Some cook radish or more exotic vegetable

definitions.note: an exotic vegetable, contrasted with the radish

indicators.note: 'some' means only part, so the letters are a portion of the phrase

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A recipe suggestion: cook radishes or something more unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: Okra, or ladies' fingers, is a green pod vegetable from tropical regions, less familiar than a radish.

clue.text: Land you'd find imaginative writer in — by no means!

definitions.text: Land you'd find imaginative writer in
definitions.note: names the first part of Never-Never Land
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the fantasy island of J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan
second meaning: an emphatic refusal, the same word said twice

explanation.surface: An author lives in a dream world, and someone protests firmly that it is not so.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrie's island was first called the Never Never Land; the doubled negative is an emphatic 'certainly not'.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Pan's island is the Never-Never Land, and repeating the word for 'not at all' gives an emphatic refusal.

clue.text: Fish aunt served in pie

indicators.note: pie is printers' slang for type spilt into a jumble, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An aunt is dished up a fish pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served' is a link; the pie is a jumble, not a pastry dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuna is a large ocean fish, much eaten tinned or as steaks.

clue.text: Oriental film disheartened gourmet

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the centre, so the middle letter goes

parts.note: E for East
a picture is a film, as in 'the pictures'

explanation.surface: A disappointing Eastern film.
explanation.walkthrough: PICTURE has seven letters, so its heart is the fourth, T.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicure is a person devoted to refined food and drink, a connoisseur of fine eating.

clue.text: Contrive to get one soul free

indicators.note: to contrive is to devise or engineer, so the letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plot to liberate a single prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: To unloose is to unfasten or release, so it works as the verb to set at liberty.

clue.text: Appoints board, one unlikely to give strong condemnation

indicators.note: an unlikely result is improbable, so the letters fall in an unexpected order

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A company names a board member who is not expected to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: Disapprobation is moral disapproval, a formal word for censure or condemnation.
